title: Umbilical Cord Prolapse: Relieve Compression and Get to Birth Fast
bottomLine: A prolapsed umbilical cord can abruptly cut fetal blood flow. Call for obstetric emergency help, relieve pressure on the presenting part using the unit's emergency protocol, position to reduce compression, and prepare for rapid delivery.
recognize: Sudden prolonged fetal bradycardia or recurrent severe decelerations after membrane rupture, especially with a palpable/visible cord, is highly concerning.
priorities: Activate emergency response, relieve cord compression, avoid handling the cord unnecessarily, and prepare for operative delivery.
assessMonitor: Continuous fetal heart rate, maternal vital signs, cord/presenting-part status, and response to decompression maneuvers.
interventions: Maintain manual elevation of presenting part if trained/ordered by protocol and use prescribed maternal positioning while transport to delivery is arranged.
medicationSafety: Do not delay mechanical decompression and emergency delivery preparation while waiting for medications.
teaching: In an emergency, explain briefly that rapid positioning and delivery are needed to protect fetal oxygenation.
delegationScope: Emergency assistance is immediate; invasive decompression maneuvers depend on training and facility policy, with obstetric team leadership.
examTrap: Pushing the cord back into the uterus instead of relieving pressure and preparing for emergency birth.
oneLinePearl: Cord prolapse: lift pressure off the cord and mobilize for delivery.

title: Uterine Tachysystole: Reduce Stimulation and Protect Fetal Oxygenation
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
bottomLine: Excessively frequent uterine contractions can reduce placental perfusion, especially when accompanied by fetal heart-rate abnormalities. Stop/reduce uterotonic stimulation per protocol, reposition, assess maternal-fetal status, and escalate promptly.
recognize: Frequent contractions with inadequate relaxation and recurrent fetal decelerations or bradycardia are concerning.
priorities: Assess contraction pattern/fetal response and follow the oxytocin/tachysystole safety algorithm.
assessMonitor: Trend contraction frequency/duration/resting tone if available, fetal heart rate, oxytocin dose, maternal BP/HR, and pain.
interventions: Discontinue/reduce oxytocin when indicated by protocol, reposition, support IV fluids/other ordered intrauterine resuscitation measures, and call obstetric team.
medicationSafety: Oxytocin is high-alert; dose changes and any tocolytic rescue must follow protocol/authorized orders.
teaching: Explain that medication may be paused if contractions become too frequent or fetal response is abnormal.
delegationScope: Fetal/contraction interpretation and oxytocin management are licensed/competency dependent; PN/LVN role varies by state/facility.
examTrap: Increasing oxytocin because cervical change is slow despite tachysystole and fetal decelerations.
oneLinePearl: Too many contractions plus fetal stress means reduce stimulation, not increase it.
sourceBasis: ACOG labor management and fetal monitoring principles

title: Uterine Rupture: Sudden Pain, Fetal Bradycardia, or Loss of Station Is an Emergency
bottomLine: Uterine rupture can cause catastrophic maternal hemorrhage and fetal hypoxia. Sudden persistent abdominal pain, abnormal fetal heart rate—often bradycardia—loss of fetal station, cessation/change of contractions, vaginal bleeding, or shock requires immediate obstetric emergency response.
recognize: Risk is higher with uterine scar or other obstetric risk factors, but fetal deterioration may be the earliest sign.
priorities: Call emergency obstetric/surgical team, assess maternal ABCs/perfusion and fetal status, stop uterotonic infusion, and prepare for urgent operative birth/resuscitation.
assessMonitor: Maternal BP/HR/mental status, bleeding, pain, uterine/contraction pattern, fetal heart rate, and fetal station if assessed by qualified clinician.
interventions: Maintain emergency IV/blood readiness and rapid transport to operative care per protocol.
medicationSafety: Stop oxytocin/uterotonics when rupture is suspected according to emergency protocol; blood products/medications are ordered under hemorrhage response.
teaching: In emergency care, provide concise explanation while prioritizing rapid intervention.
delegationScope: Emergency support is immediate; diagnosis/operative decisions are obstetric provider responsibilities.
examTrap: Waiting for obvious external bleeding before escalating severe fetal bradycardia and maternal pain.
oneLinePearl: Uterine rupture may announce itself through the fetal heart rate before visible hemorrhage.
sourceBasis: ACOG obstetric emergency and VBAC safety principles

title: Shoulder Dystocia: Call for Help and Use the Team Algorithm—Never Fundal Pressure
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Coordinated Care
bottomLine: When the fetal head delivers but the shoulders do not, shoulder dystocia is an obstetric emergency. Call for help, note the time, assist with ordered maneuvers, prepare neonatal resuscitation, and never apply fundal pressure.
recognize: Retraction of the delivered head ('turtle sign') and failure of shoulders to deliver with usual traction are cues.
priorities: Activate the shoulder-dystocia team and assist with standardized maneuvers directed by the obstetric clinician.
assessMonitor: Track timing, maneuvers, maternal condition, and neonatal status after birth.
interventions: Assist with maternal positioning such as McRoberts/suprapubic pressure if within trained role and directed; avoid fundal pressure.
medicationSafety: Medication is not the primary fix for mechanical shoulder impaction.
redFlags: Failure of shoulders to deliver after head
teaching: After stabilization, explain what happened and expected maternal/newborn follow-up.
delegationScope: Maneuver performance depends on training/role; PN/LVN provides assigned emergency support and documentation/handoff.
examTrap: Applying fundal pressure to push the shoulders through.
oneLinePearl: Shoulder dystocia is a team mechanical emergency—suprapubic, not fundal, pressure when directed.

title: Amniotic Fluid Embolism: Sudden Hypoxia, Hypotension, and Coagulopathy Need Immediate Resuscitation
bottomLine: Sudden respiratory distress/hypoxemia, hypotension/cardiovascular collapse, altered consciousness, and rapid coagulopathy during labor or soon after birth can indicate amniotic fluid embolism. Activate maternal resuscitation and massive hemorrhage/critical-care response immediately.
recognize: Collapse can be abrupt and may be followed by DIC/hemorrhage.
priorities: ABCs, emergency obstetric/anesthesia/critical-care activation, CPR if needed, oxygenation/ventilation support, and hemorrhage readiness.
assessMonitor: Continuous hemodynamics/oxygenation, neurologic status, bleeding, fetal status if undelivered, and coagulation/labs.
interventions: Support resuscitation, rapid blood-product availability, and operative delivery decisions under team leadership.
medicationSafety: Resuscitation medications and blood products follow emergency protocols; no single medication confirms/treats the diagnosis.
teaching: After survival/stabilization, provide trauma-informed explanation and support.
delegationScope: Emergency response roles follow competency; diagnosis and critical-care strategy are provider-led.
examTrap: Waiting for a diagnostic test before treating sudden cardiopulmonary collapse.
oneLinePearl: AFE is a resuscitation diagnosis—treat the collapse first.

title: Intraamniotic Infection: Maternal Fever Plus Labor Findings Requires Prompt Treatment
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Maternal intrapartum fever with fetal/maternal tachycardia, uterine tenderness, purulent/foul fluid, or other infection findings can indicate intraamniotic infection. Notify the obstetric team promptly and support ordered antibiotics and delivery management.
recognize: Fever in labor has differential causes, but infection must be evaluated rather than ignored.
priorities: Assess maternal vital signs, fetal status, membrane status/fluid findings, and sepsis cues; escalate promptly.
assessMonitor: Temperature, BP/HR, uterine tenderness, fetal heart rate, fluid odor/appearance, and ordered labs.
interventions: Administer ordered antimicrobials/fluids and maintain fetal/maternal monitoring according to plan.
medicationSafety: Antibiotic regimen is prescriber/protocol driven; verify allergies and timing.
teaching: Explain need for antibiotics and newborn observation when infection is suspected.
delegationScope: Routine vitals may be delegated; infection interpretation and obstetric escalation require licensed judgment.
examTrap: Treating intrapartum fever with acetaminophen alone without infection evaluation.
oneLinePearl: Fever in labor is a cause-finding problem, not just a temperature-control problem.
sourceBasis: ACOG current clinical update on suspected intraamniotic infection

title: Meconium-Stained Fluid: Prepare for Newborn Support, Do Not Perform Routine Unnecessary Suction
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
Safe and Effective Care Environment: Coordinated Care
bottomLine: Meconium-stained amniotic fluid requires appropriate neonatal-resuscitation readiness and fetal assessment. Current neonatal resuscitation focuses on effective ventilation/resuscitation rather than routine invasive suction solely because meconium is present.
recognize: Thick meconium plus abnormal fetal status or a nonvigorous newborn increases need for skilled neonatal support.
priorities: Notify/prepare the neonatal team and monitor fetal/newborn transition according to protocol.
assessMonitor: Fetal heart pattern, fluid character, newborn tone/respiratory effort/heart rate at birth.
interventions: Support the 2025 AHA/AAP neonatal-resuscitation sequence directed by trained personnel.
medicationSafety: No prophylactic medication replaces resuscitation readiness.
teaching: Explain that the newborn team may be present because meconium can be associated with breathing problems.
delegationScope: Neonatal resuscitation roles require current competency; PN/LVN participates only within certified role.
examTrap: Automatically performing deep tracheal suction before establishing effective ventilation solely due to meconium.
oneLinePearl: Meconium means prepare for resuscitation; ventilation remains the priority when the newborn needs help.

title: Neuraxial Analgesia: Sudden Maternal Hypotension Can Reduce Fetal Perfusion
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
bottomLine: Epidural/spinal analgesia can cause maternal hypotension, which may reduce uteroplacental perfusion and contribute to fetal heart-rate abnormalities. Assess maternal-fetal status, reposition, support ordered fluids/vasopressor measures, and notify anesthesia/obstetric team promptly.
recognize: Dizziness, nausea, pallor, low BP, fetal deceleration/bradycardia after neuraxial dosing are concerning.
priorities: Position to support venous return/uteroplacental perfusion, reassess BP/fetal heart rate, and call anesthesia/obstetric support.
assessMonitor: BP/HR, sensory/motor block, respiratory status, fetal heart rate, and symptoms after dosing.
interventions: Follow neuraxial hypotension protocol and fall/mobility precautions.
medicationSafety: Vasopressors/boluses and neuraxial medication dosing are anesthesia/protocol directed; monitor for high block and respiratory depression.
teaching: Call for assistance before standing and report difficulty breathing, severe weakness, or dizziness.
delegationScope: Neuraxial drug administration and management are credential dependent; PN/LVN may monitor/support within policy.
examTrap: Leaving a hypotensive patient supine while waiting for the anesthesiologist.
oneLinePearl: After neuraxial analgesia, maternal pressure and fetal response are linked.

title: Persistent Fetal Bradycardia: Correct Reversible Causes While Mobilizing the Team
bottomLine: Persistent fetal bradycardia/prolonged deceleration can reflect cord compression, maternal hypotension, tachysystole, abruption, uterine rupture, or other acute compromise. Begin intrauterine resuscitation measures and emergency obstetric escalation immediately while seeking the cause.
recognize: A sustained low fetal heart rate, especially with maternal symptoms or after membrane rupture/uterotonic/neuraxial events, is high priority.
priorities: Call for help, reposition, stop oxytocin when indicated, assess maternal BP/bleeding/uterus, and prepare for urgent delivery if unresolved.
assessMonitor: Fetal tracing, contraction pattern, maternal BP/HR, bleeding, pain, recent medications/procedures, and cord concerns.
interventions: Implement the unit's fetal-resuscitation algorithm under obstetric leadership.
medicationSafety: Do not reflexively give oxygen to every laboring patient without indication/order; correct the identified maternal/fetal cause using current protocol.
teaching: Provide concise reassurance/explanation while the team intervenes rapidly.
delegationScope: Fetal tracing interpretation and emergency management require qualified obstetric clinicians; PN/LVN assists within policy.
examTrap: Documenting the bradycardia and waiting for the next routine reassessment interval.
oneLinePearl: Persistent fetal bradycardia is a now problem—intervene and mobilize simultaneously.
sourceBasis: ACOG fetal heart-rate monitoring and intrapartum emergency principles

title: After Operative Vaginal or Cesarean Birth: Handoff Must Carry Hemorrhage and Newborn Risks
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Coordinated Care
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: After urgent cesarean or operative vaginal birth, handoff must clearly communicate indication, blood loss/hemorrhage risk, anesthesia, medications, lacerations/incisions, uterine tone/bleeding, maternal complications, newborn transition/resuscitation, and pending labs/treatments.
recognize: Emergency birth increases risk of fragmented handoff because multiple teams are involved.
priorities: Use closed-loop structured handoff for both mother and newborn and explicitly identify unresolved risks.
assessMonitor: Maternal bleeding/tone/vitals/pain, anesthesia recovery, incision/perineum, urine output, newborn respiratory/temperature/glucose risks as indicated.
interventions: Continue ordered postpartum and newborn surveillance and escalate deviations promptly.
medicationSafety: Reconcile uterotonics, antibiotics, analgesics, anticoagulation/VTE plan, and newborn medications given/pending.
teaching: Explain postpartum warning signs and newborn monitoring needs after stabilization.
delegationScope: Structured handoff is team responsibility; initial comprehensive postpartum/newborn assessment follows licensed role policy.
examTrap: Treating transfer from operating room as routine postpartum handoff without naming blood loss, anesthesia, or unresolved neonatal issues.
oneLinePearl: Emergency birth is not over at delivery—the risks must survive the handoff.
